message.content: A mechanical water pump moves water uphill by converting rotational or reciprocating energy into pressure that overcomes gravity. In a typical centrifugal pump, an electric motor or engine spins an impeller, a disk with curved blades. As the impeller rotates, it flings water outward from its center, creating a low-pressure zone at the inlet. This pressure difference draws more water into the pump from the source. The water gains kinetic energy as it travels along the spinning impeller blades, and the volute, a spiral casing surrounding the impeller, converts that velocity into pressure. This pressure is strong enough to push the water up through the discharge pipe and against the force of gravity to reach a higher elevation. The pump does not pull the water; it pushes it, and the continuous transfer of energy from the motor to the water sustains the flow uphill.
